# The question {.divider background-color="#008CB7"}

[Act I · One variable]{.act}

## You have 171 numbers. Now what?

Annual earnings for 171 full-time working women aged 30. A column of 171 dollar
amounts tells you nothing at a glance.

. . .

**Univariate summary** is how we compress that column into a handful of numbers — and
a few pictures — that reveal its center, its spread, and its shape.

::: {.notes}
Univariate = a single variable. Before any modeling, you summarize. This chapter is the
toolkit: summary statistics for the numbers, charts for the shape.
:::

## Where we're going

::: {.incremental}
- **Summarize** a variable with the mean, median, spread, and shape statistics
- **Visualize** numerical data — box plots, histograms, density, line charts
- **Compare** categories with bar and pie charts
- **Transform** skewed data with logarithms and z-scores
- **Smooth** time series with moving averages and seasonal adjustment
:::

## Six ideas anchor this chapter

::: {.incremental}
- **Mean vs. median** — the average, pulled by outliers; vs. the honest middle value
- **Standard deviation** — the typical distance of a point from the mean
- **Quartiles & IQR** — $Q_1$, $Q_2$, $Q_3$ split the data in four; IQR $= Q_3 - Q_1$
- **Skewness** — asymmetry; $> 1$ means a long right tail
- **Kurtosis** — tail heaviness; excess $> 0$ means more outliers than a bell curve
- **Z-score** — $z_i = (x_i - \bar{x})/s$, a value rescaled to "standard deviations from the mean"
:::

[For skewed economic data, the median is usually the more honest "typical" value.]{.takeaway .fragment}

# From numbers to a shape {.divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Act II · The investigation]{.act}

## Start with the numbers: center, spread, shape

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-6|8|9"}
import pandas as pd                          # tabular data
from scipy import stats                      # skewness & kurtosis

# dataset: 171 full-time working women aged 30, 2010 (earnings in $)
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_EARNINGS.DTA"
data = pd.read_stata(url)                    # read the Stata .dta into a DataFrame

data[["earnings"]].describe().round(0)       # count, mean, std, min, quartiles, max
stats.skew(data["earnings"]), stats.kurtosis(data["earnings"])  # shape: 1.71, 4.32 (excess)
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
pandas gives center and spread in one call; scipy.stats adds shape. scipy returns EXCESS
kurtosis by default (raw − 3), so 0 is the bell-curve baseline.
:::

## The mean sits above the median — a telltale of skew

::: {.incremental}
- **Mean $= \$41{,}413$** but **median $= \$36{,}000$** — a \$5,413 gap (15%).
- **Std. dev. $= \$25{,}527$** — 62% of the mean: enormous spread.
- **$Q_1 = \$25{,}000$, $Q_3 = \$49{,}000$** → IQR $= \$24{,}000$ holds the middle half.
- **Skewness $= 1.71$** ($> 1$ = highly skewed); **excess kurtosis $= 4.32$** (heavy tails).
:::

[A handful of high earners (max \$172,000) drag the mean up; report the median as "typical."]{.takeaway .fragment}

## The box plot draws those statistics in one picture

![Box = $Q_1$ to $Q_3$ (the middle 50%); red line = median; dots on the right = high-earner outliers.](figures/box.png)

[The median sits left of center and the right whisker is long — the chart *is* the skew.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## A histogram shows the whole distribution — bin width is a choice

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-5|7|8-9|10"}
import pandas as pd                          # tabular data
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt               # plotting

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_EARNINGS.DTA"
earnings = pd.read_stata(url)["earnings"]    # the single variable

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))         # two panels side by side
ax[0].hist(earnings, bins=12, color="#22d3ee", edgecolor="black")  # wider bins → coarse shape
ax[1].hist(earnings, bins=25, color="#22d3ee", edgecolor="black")  # narrower bins → fine detail
plt.show()                                   # render the histograms
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

## Wide bins give the shape; narrow bins give the detail

![The same 171 earnings at two bin widths. Both show the long right tail; the narrower bins reveal clustering around \$25k–\$45k.](figures/hist.png)

[Always try more than one bin width — each answers a different question.]{.takeaway .fragment}

[Sort categories before plotting so the ranking reads instantly.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## Categorical data: count, then show the shares

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-5|7|8|9-10"}
import pandas as pd                          # tabular data
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt               # plotting

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_FISHING.DTA"
data = pd.read_stata(url)                    # 1,182 recreational fishers

counts = data["mode"].value_counts()         # frequency of each fishing site
counts / counts.sum() * 100                  # relative frequency (% of total)
plt.pie(counts, labels=counts.index, autopct="%1.1f%%")  # each slice = a site's share
plt.show()                                   # render the pie chart
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
value_counts() builds the frequency table; normalize=True (or dividing by the sum) gives
relative frequencies. Boat-based modes (charter 38% + private 35%) are ~74% of choices.
:::

## Boat fishing dominates the 1,182 choices

![Charter (38.2%) + private (35.4%) = 74% of fishers choose a boat; pier and beach split the rest.](figures/pie.png)

[Pie charts show shares; for many categories a sorted bar chart compares them more cleanly.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## Logs tame right-skewed economic data

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-3|5-6|8|9|10"}
import numpy as np                           # natural logarithm
import pandas as pd                          # tabular data
from scipy import stats                      # skewness

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_EARNINGS.DTA"
data = pd.read_stata(url)                    # load the 171 earnings

data["ln_earnings"] = np.log(data["earnings"])   # log-transform the skewed variable
stats.skew(data["earnings"])                      # 1.71  → strong right skew
stats.skew(data["ln_earnings"])                   # -0.91 → nearly symmetric
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Logs convert multiplicative, right-skewed data (income, prices, wealth) toward symmetry.
On the log scale the mean (10.46) and median (10.49) nearly coincide. Logs need positive data.
:::

## The log scale collapses the long tail toward a bell

![Panel A: earnings in dollars, strongly right-skewed. Panel B: log(earnings), roughly symmetric — skew falls from 1.71 to −0.91.](figures/logtransform.png)

[Many tests assume a bell shape; the log transform is how skewed economic data gets there.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## Time series need smoothing to reveal the trend

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|3-4|5|7|8"}
import pandas as pd                          # tabular data

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_MONTHLYHOMESALES.DTA"
data = pd.read_stata(url).query("year >= 2005")   # monthly U.S. home sales, 2005+
data = data.sort_values("daten")             # ensure time order

data["ma11"] = data["exsales"].rolling(11, center=True).mean()  # 11-month moving average
data[["exsales", "ma11"]].describe().round(0)     # raw (noisy) vs smoothed series
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
A moving average averages each point with its neighbors, cancelling month-to-month noise.
Seasonal adjustment instead removes the recurring summer-peak / winter-trough pattern.
:::

## Smoothing reveals the 2007–2011 housing crash

![Raw monthly sales zig-zag with the seasons; the 11-month moving average (red) and seasonal adjustment (green) expose the boom–bust–recovery cycle.](figures/timeseries.png)

[A moving average cancels seasonal noise; seasonal adjustment removes the predictable pattern itself.]{.takeaway .fragment}

# Reading it right {.divider background-color="#C21E72"}

[Act III · The resolution]{.act}

## Choose the summary that matches the shape

[Objection.]{.objection} "Just report the mean and a histogram — that's what a summary is."

. . .

[Response.]{.rebuttal} The right summary depends on the **shape**. For skewed earnings, the
mean overstates the "typical" value, so lead with the **median** and **IQR**. A histogram's
story changes with its **bin width**. And a raw time series hides its trend until you **smooth** it.

[Match the tool to the data: skew → median & logs; categories → bars; time → moving averages.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## What to carry forward

::: {.incremental}
- Summarize center (**mean/median**), spread (**std. dev., IQR**), and shape (**skew, kurtosis**).
- For skewed economic data the **median** is the honest center; the **mean** is pulled by outliers.
- Pick the chart for the data type: **histogram/box/line** (numerical), **bar/pie** (categorical).
- **Logs** symmetrize right-skewed data; **z-scores** put different variables on one scale.
- For time series, **moving averages** smooth noise and **seasonal adjustment** removes recurring patterns.
:::
